newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: IMF needs to rebuild confidence in Thailand.
newsitem.headline: IMF needs to rebuild confidence in Thailand.

text.p: The big job for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Thailand is rebuilding investor confidence to slow potentially heavy capital flight when exchange controls are lifted, economic analysts said.
The Thai government is expected to announce a package of measures by August 5 to allow it to qualify for a standby credit line from the IMF.
These measures are widely seen as including tighter fiscal and monetary policies and an end to the capital controls imposed in mid-May to curb offshore speculation in the baht.
"The IMF will impose some sort of greater discipline on the Thai authorities to do what is necessary," said Wong Yit Fan, chief economist, Southeast Asia at Standard Chartered Bank.

"But more important is the need to manage investor perceptions. They (investors) need to see the IMF backing the Thai government, this is more important than the actual details of any economic measures," he said.
Analysts and traders in the offshore baht markets widely forecast that the baht will fall sharply in an initial knee jerk reaction to the lifting of capital controls.
A senior dealer at a Hong Kong-based bank said, "Some people in the market are saying the baht could go to 40 (to the dollar)."
Confidence in the baht was not helped on Friday when ratings agency Standard & Poor's Corp placed Thailand's "A" long-term foreign currency rating on creditwatch.

The onshore baht rate ended Friday at 31.85 to the dollar, down just 0.5 percent on the week but still 20 percent below levels seen before the de facto devaluation on July 2. The offshore rate ended the week basically unchanged at 32.00 to the U.S. dollar.
Some economists do believe confidence can be restored quickly as Thailand had already gone some way toward tackling its economic problems before the baht crisis.

Figures released by the Thai central bank on Thursday showed the current account deficit down to $22.8 billion in May from $38 billion in April and nearly $36 billion in May 1996. "It wouldn't take them (the IMF) more than six months to see the situation begin to turn around," Wong said.
But other economists, fearful of the impact of an austere economic package from the IMF on the fragile condition of many Thai companies, think it may take longer.

"I think we may be talking about years. It's not going to be easy for domestic companies to take the brunt of any economic restraint measures," said Jacqueline Ong, regional economist at the consultancy firm I.D.E.A.
Along the way, it looks like Thailand may have to shed its tag as an Asian tiger economy.
The new finance minister, Thanong Bidaya, has already forecast about four percent growth in 1997, with other private sector economists looking for a more modest three percent rise.

Those forecasts would have the Thai economy growing at its slowest rate since the early 1960s. The country recorded 6.4 percent gross domestic product growth in 1996 and 8.6 percent the previous year.
"The economy is already slowing, but maybe in IMF eyes that is still not sufficient," Ong said.
"It may mean that Thailand has got to shift its ambitions for higher value added exports to later years," she said.
